result:
I now have a complete picture of both the write-time indexing path and the query-time path. Here's how it works.

## Write side: keeping the index in step

When someone edits an issue title, the mutation goes through `updateIssue` in `src/server/services/issue-service.ts`. That function runs the standard write gates — `assertOrgScope(actor, input.orgId)` (tenant check), `assertCan(actor, "issue:update", issueResource(before))` (permission check), `assertNotArchived(...)` — then calls `issueRepo.updateIssue(input)` to persist the new title in the primary `issues` table. Immediately after the write succeeds, it calls `emit("issue.updated", { ...actorEnvelope(actor), issueId: after.id, projectId: after.projectId, changedFields: [...] })`.

`emit` is defined in `src/lib/event-bus.ts`, an in-process typed pub/sub bus. It does not carry the new title in the payload — only identifiers and which fields changed. Every subscriber for `"issue.updated"` is invoked, and handlers are isolated (`event-bus.ts` catches per-handler errors via `errorSinks` so one throwing handler can't break the emit or its siblings).

The search indexer subscribes to this at process start. `src/server/services/event-registry.ts` calls `registerSearchListeners()` (exported from `src/server/services/search-service.ts`) once from `src/instrumentation.ts`, guarded by a `detach` flag so a dev hot-reload can't double-subscribe. Inside `registerSearchListeners`, the handler for `"issue.updated"` is:

```
subscribe("issue.updated", async (payload) => {
  const issue = await issueRepo.findIssueById(payload.orgId, payload.issueId);
  if (issue) await indexIssue(payload.orgId, issue);
}),
```

Note it re-reads the row from `issueRepo` rather than trusting anything in the event payload — the comment above `registerSearchListeners` explains this is deliberate, so a partially-applied write is never indexed as if it fully succeeded. `indexIssue` then calls `searchRepo.upsertSearchDocument(orgId, "issue", issue.id, [issue.title, issue.description ?? ""].join("\n"), issue.projectId)` in `src/server/repositories/search-repository.ts`. That function looks up an existing row by `(orgId, subjectKind, subjectId)` and either updates its `content`/`projectId`/`indexedAt` or inserts a new row into the `searchIndex` table — so what's actually stored in the searchable copy is just a newline-joined blob of `title + description` per subject, tagged with kind/id/org/project and a timestamp, not the full issue record. This whole path is asynchronous but fires synchronously off the same event-loop turn as the write (no queue in between for this particular path), which is why a colleague searching moments later already sees it. There's also a belt-and-suspenders `"search.reindex_requested"` event with the same re-read-and-`indexIssue` handler, used for drift repair (see `src/server/jobs/search-reindex-job.ts`, which walks an org's issues/comments/projects and re-derives the index after a bulk import or a drift alarm), and a `search.reindex_requested`-independent `countIndexed` used by that same drift check.

## Query side: what a search request goes through

A query enters through one of the equivalent front doors — the Server Action `searchAction` in `src/actions/search/search.ts`, the JSON route `src/app/api/search/route.ts` (used by the command palette for cancellable per-keystroke fetches), or directly from `src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/search/page.tsx`. All three parse the raw input against `searchQuerySchema` (`src/schemas/search.ts`), then call `search(actor, input)` in `search-service.ts`.

Inside `search()`, in order:

1. `assertOrgScope(actor, input.orgId)` — throws `TenantScopeError` if the actor isn't scoped to the org being searched.
2. `assertCan(actor, "issue:read", orgResource(input.orgId))` — throws `PermissionDeniedError` (`code: "forbidden"`) if the actor lacks read permission.
3. `consumeRateLimit(input.orgId, "search:query")` from `src/lib/rate-limit.ts` — a per-org, per-bucket token bucket (capacity/refill scaled by plan via `getPlanLimits`). If the bucket is exhausted, `verdict.allowed` is `false` and the function throws `Search rate limit reached; try again after ${verdict.resetAt}` — this is the "perfectly valid-looking query gets refused" case: correct tenant, correct permissions, well-formed query, but too many requests too fast for that org.
4. It loads the org and evaluates the `advanced_search` feature flag via `isEnabled(...)` from `src/lib/feature-flags.ts`.
5. If the query text contains a `:` (field-scoped syntax like `status:done`) and `advanced_search` is not enabled for that org/plan, it throws `"Field-scoped search is not included in this plan"` — a second refusal path for an otherwise well-formed query.
6. Only after all that does it call `searchRepo.searchDocuments(input)`, which runs a tenant-scoped `LIKE %q%` filter over the `searchIndex.content` column (plus optional `kinds`/`projectId` filters), ordered by `indexedAt`/`id` for keyset pagination.
7. Results are mapped back into `SearchHit`s — `title` is just the first line of the stored `content` blob, and `snippet` is computed on the fly by `snippetAround()`, which does a case-insensitive substring search around the match with a fixed character radius.

So the colleague's query for the new title succeeds because the `"issue.updated"` handler already rewrote the `searchIndex` row's `content` field synchronously after the title change; the query path would refuse an otherwise-valid request only if the org's search rate limit is currently exhausted, or if the query uses `:` field syntax the org's plan doesn't include.
